**Research note: PostgreSQL identifier length, column limit, and max_connections**

Identifiers such as table, column, and constraint names are limited to 63 bytes by default. The manual says the system uses no more than NAMEDATALEN-1 bytes of an identifier, that NAMEDATALEN defaults to 64, and that longer names are accepted in commands but truncated (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). The limit counts bytes, not characters, so multi-byte UTF-8 names reach it sooner. The constant can only be raised by recompiling, by editing src/include/pg_config_manual.h (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html).

A table can have at most 1,600 columns. The limits appendix states this figure, but also says the real ceiling is lower because each row must fit in one 8,192-byte heap page (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). The manual's example is that 1,600 int columns fit in a page at 6,400 bytes, while 1,600 bigint columns at 12,800 bytes do not. Dropped columns also count toward the 1,600 limit, so a table that has had columns dropped can run out of slots sooner than expected (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). For a wide schema, the practical limit depends on the column types, not on 1,600 alone.

The default max_connections is 100. The configuration reference says the default is "typically 100 connections, but might be less if your kernel settings will not support it," as determined during initdb. The parameter can only be set at server start, and PostgreSQL allocates shared memory and other resources in proportion to it (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html).

**Recommendation:** Keep the schema well under the column ceiling, and size the row width against the 8 KB page limit rather than the 1,600 figure. Put a connection pooler in front of the database and keep max_connections modest, because every extra connection costs memory and the pool, not max_connections, should set how many clients reach the server.

**Research note: default memory and WAL settings in PostgreSQL**

I checked the defaults against the official PostgreSQL 18 documentation, which is the current version. The first two answers come from the resource-consumption chapter. The third comes from the WAL configuration chapter.

**work_mem** defaults to 4 MB. The docs state that "the default value is four megabytes (4MB)" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). This limit applies per sort or hash operation, not per connection, so a single query with several sorts can use several multiples of it.

**shared_buffers** defaults to 128 MB, but the docs describe this as typical rather than guaranteed. The default "is typically 128 megabytes (128MB), but might be less if your kernel settings will not support it (as determined during initdb)" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). On a fresh install, check what `initdb` actually chose, because a constrained kernel can lower it.

**max_wal_size** defaults to 1 GB. The docs state that "the default is 1 GB" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). This is a soft target that controls how much WAL can accumulate between automatic checkpoints. It is not a hard cap, so WAL can temporarily exceed it under heavy write load.

Two caveats apply. These values are from the PostgreSQL 18 docs, and older releases may have different defaults, so confirm against the docs for the version you run. I did not check the release notes for changes between versions.

**Recommendation:** Leave `work_mem` at 4 MB globally and raise it per session or per role for known heavy reporting queries, rather than raising it server-wide. Before changing `max_wal_size`, measure checkpoint frequency and write volume first, since raising it lengthens crash recovery time.

**Research note: analytics side-store next to PostgreSQL (DuckDB vs. SQLite), and MERGE on PostgreSQL 15**

**DuckDB memory default.** DuckDB's memory management write-up states that the default `memory_limit` is 80% of the system's physical RAM, so a 16 GB machine gets about 12.8 GB (source: https://duckdb.org/2024/07/09/memory-management). I did not confirm how this behaves inside containers, so set `memory_limit` explicitly on constrained hosts.

**SQLite file size.** The SQLite limits page gives the maximum database file size as 4294967294 pages. At the largest page size of 65536 bytes, that is about 281 terabytes, but at the default 4096-byte page size the same page count gives only about 17.5 TB (source: https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html). The effective ceiling therefore depends on page size, and the filesystem may impose a lower cap.

**MERGE on PostgreSQL.** The MERGE command first appeared in PostgreSQL 15. The 15 release announcement says the release "adds the SQL standard MERGE command, which lets you write conditional SQL statements that can include INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE actions within a single statement" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-15-released-2526/). If your server is older than 15, MERGE is not available until you upgrade.

**Recommendation.** For analytical scans over large columnar data, DuckDB is the better side-store, as long as you set its memory limit for your host. SQLite suits a simple embedded file store, but its practical size depends on page size, so check that before relying on the 281 TB figure.


**Research note: TLS versions, host naming and HTTP status codes**

**TLS 1.3.** TLS 1.3 was specified in RFC 8446, published in August 2018 as a Proposed Standard. The RFC Editor page for it now carries the banner "This RFC is now obsolete, see" and points to RFC 9846, whose title is again "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3" and whose abstract says it obsoletes RFC 8446 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8446; source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9846). A guideline should therefore cite RFC 9846 as the current specification and RFC 8446 as its predecessor. I did not confirm the exact publication date of RFC 9846; its page shows only a 2026 copyright notice.

**DNS label length.** The maximum length of a single label is 63 octets. RFC 1035, section 2.3.4 "Size limits," lists labels at "63 octets or less" and whole names at "255 octets or less" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035). The figure is not in RFC 1034, which the question named. The search results pointed to RFC 1035 as well, so I read that primary text directly.

**"I'm a teapot."** The status code 418 "I'm a teapot" is defined by RFC 2324, the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0), written by L. Masinter and dated 1 April 1998. Section 2.3.2 states: "Any attempt to brew coffee with a teapot should result in the error code '418 I'm a teapot'" (source: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2324). The RFC is an informational April Fools' document with no formal standing, so it should not be treated as a normative source for HTTP status codes. I did not read the primary text of the 2017 Node.js removal discussions; that history comes only from secondary search summaries.

**Recommendation.** Cite RFC 9846 (with RFC 8446 noted as obsolete) when the guideline names TLS 1.3, and cite RFC 1035 section 2.3.4 for the 63-octet label limit. Do not rely on 418 for production APIs, since it is a joke code with no standing, and state that explicitly if a team wants to use it.

**Research note: timeouts, grace periods, and the Docker bridge subnet**

**Lambda timeout.** The maximum timeout for a Lambda function invocation is 900 seconds (15 minutes). The AWS page states that "Timeout is the maximum amount of time in seconds that a Lambda function can run," with a default of 3 seconds and a ceiling of 900 seconds (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). The same page notes an exception for functions on AWS Lambda Managed Instances, where asynchronous and event source mapping invocations allow up to 5,400 seconds, so the runbook should say which function type it means.

**Kubernetes grace period.** The default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` for a Pod is 30 seconds. The Kubernetes lifecycle documentation says, in its Pod termination flow, that "The default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting is 30 seconds," and that "By default, all deletes are graceful within 30 seconds" (source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/). Because preStop hooks run inside this window, a runbook that expects longer shutdowns should set the field explicitly.

**Docker default bridge subnet.** The default `docker0` bridge uses 172.17.0.0/16. I could not confirm this on Docker's own documentation. The bridge driver page and the `dockerd` reference name `docker0` as the default bridge but do not give its subnet. The value comes from a third-party engineering blog, which states that "Docker's default bridge (`docker0`) uses `172.17.0.0/16` by default" (source: https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-20-change-default-docker-bridge-subnet/view). Treat it as likely but unverified against primary sources, and check it on a real host with `docker network inspect bridge` before writing it into the runbook.

**Recommendation.** Cite the AWS and Kubernetes pages for the timeout and grace-period values, since both are official and were read directly. Mark the Docker subnet as needing host verification, and avoid hard-coding it in the runbook, because hosts with overlapping 172.17.x.x networks often change it.

**Research note: test and tooling defaults**

**Vitest per-test timeout.** The default `testTimeout` in Vitest is 5,000 ms in Node.js, and 15,000 ms when `browser.enabled` is true. The default is documented as "Default timeout of a test in milliseconds" (source: https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout). A value of 0 disables the timeout, per the same search summary, but I did not confirm that on the fetched page, so treat it as unverified.

**First Linux kernel with Rust in mainline.** Initial Rust support entered the mainline tree in Linux 6.1. The jcarr blog post says the initial Rust support "is now targeted for 6.1" and that the first merge into mainline "was completed on October 3rd" (source: https://jcarr.codeberg.page/blog/posts/2022/rust_linux_kernel.html). This is a secondary source. I tried the Phoronix article on the 6.1 merge and it returned HTTP 403, and the kernel's own Rust documentation page did not state a version, so the primary-source confirmation is still missing. Rust support is still optional at build time.

**PostgreSQL `statement_timeout`.** The default is 0, which disables the timeout. The official PostgreSQL documentation for client connection defaults says "A value of zero (the default) disables the timeout" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html). A unitless value is interpreted as milliseconds. A third-party mirror of the parameter reference agrees on the default of 0 ms (source: https://postgresqlco.nf/en/doc/param/statement_timeout).

**Recommendation.** For Vitest, keep the 5-second Node default and override per test or per suite only where a test legitimately needs longer, instead of raising the global value. For PostgreSQL, the server default of no timeout is safe for migrations but should be set explicitly per role or application connection for web request paths, since the server will not abort a runaway query on its own.
